Kumano Sankeimichi | includes = | criteria = {{UNESCO WHS type|(ii)(iv)(vi)}}(ii)(iv)(vi) | ID = dd42bis | year = 2004 | extension = 2016 | area = {{convert|506.4|ha|sqmi|abbr=on}} | buffer_zone = {{convert|12100|ha|sqmi|abbr=on}} | website = https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/dd42/ }} | location = {{ill|Mie Prefecture|en|Mie Prefecture|WD=Q128196|lt=Mie Prefecture|1=Mie Prefecture}}, {{ill|Nara Prefecture|en|Nara Prefecture|WD=Q131287|lt=Nara Prefecture|1=Nara Prefecture}} and {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|en|Wakayama Prefecture|WD=Q131314|lt=Wakayama Prefecture|1=Wakayama Prefecture}} | image_size = 600 | alt = A map showing the main routes of the Kumano Kodo across the Kii Peninsula of Japan. | name = Kumano Kodō (熊野古道) }} The '''{{nihongo|Kumano Kodō|熊野古道}}''' is a series of ancient {{ill|Pilgrimage|en|Pilgrimage|WD=Q1644573|lt=Pilgrimage|1=Pilgrimage}} routes that crisscross the [[Kii Peninsula]], the largest peninsula of {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|WD=Q17|lt=Japan|1=Japan}}. These mountainous trails are used by pilgrims to the "[[Kumano shrine|Kumano Sanzan]]" (熊野三山) - the Three Grand Shrines of Kumano: [[Kumano Hongū Taisha]] (熊野本宮大社), [[Kumano Nachi Taisha]] (熊野那智大社) and [[Kumano Hayatama Taisha]] (熊野速玉大社). These three shrines are the holiest sites of the ancient {{ill|Syncretism|en|Syncretism|WD=Q172904|lt=syncretic|1=Syncretism}} Kumano religion. It has been visited by pilgrims seeking healing and salvation as a site of religious significance for over a thousand years. People with backgrounds from peasants to {{ill|Emperor of Japan|en|Emperor of Japan|WD=Q208233|lt=emperors|1=Emperor of Japan}} would visit the region while guided by [[Shugendō]] monks. In July 2004, some of the roads of the Kumano Kodō and the shrines of the Kumano Sanzan, along with {{ill|Mount Kōya|en|Mount Kōya|WD=Q535065|lt=Koyasan|1=Mount Kōya}} and Yoshino and {{ill|Mount Ōmine|en|Mount Ōmine|WD=Q3695989|lt=Ōmine|1=Mount Ōmine}}, were registered as [[:en:World Heritage|World Heritage]] sites together as the "{{ill|Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range|en|Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range|WD=Q611345|lt=Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range|1=Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range}}".{{cite web | last = UNESCO | title = Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range | url=https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/dd42 | date = 2004-07-07 | access-date = 2007-dd-30}} == History == The Kumano Kodō has been used for more than 1,000 years for the purpose of Kumano worship, which flourished as the largest sacred site in Japan during the Middle Ages.例えば、かつて十津川街道として知られていたルートは[[:en:国道168号|国道168号]]線に吸収されている。紀伊路（大阪-田辺）が登録外であるのも、[[県道]]や登山道などとして改修・拡幅されたことによる。なお、世界遺産に登録されたルートでも、大辺路・伊勢路の大部分は[[国道42号]]線と重複している。 In modern times, after its status as Japan's largest sacred site was replaced by that of [[Ise Grand Shrine|Ise Shrine]], it began to become part of the pilgrimages of the 33 sacred sites of the [[Kannon|Kannon]] in the western part of Japan. Nevertheless, the Kumano Kodō remains as a busy foot pilgrimage in its own right.並行している例として、中辺路と[[国道3dd号]]線、{{ill|Japan Railways Group|en|Japan Railways Group|WD=Q864495|lt=JR|1=Japan Railways Group}}[[:en:紀勢本線|紀勢本線]]・[[国道42号]]線の紀伊半島部分と大辺路・伊勢路がある。また、小辺路や大峯奥駈道のような例外もある。 The area around Kumano was a place of nature worship, as mentioned in the [[Nihon Shoki]] (Chronicles of Japan). The three Kumano mountains were worshipped by people from all walks of life, from emperors to aristocrats and commoners. In the {{ill|Muromachi period|en|Muromachi period|WD=Q334845|lt=Muromachi period|1=Muromachi period}} (1333-1573), Kumano pilgrimages became popular among samurai and common people and not just aristocrats, and were so frequent and continuous that they were even called a "pilgrimage of ants". In the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period|1=Edo period}} (1603-1867), Kumano pilgrimages, along with {{ill|Ise, Mie|en|Ise, Mie|WD=Q328067|lt=Ise|1=Ise, Mie}} pilgrimages, are said to have become widely practiced by the general public. At one time, 800 people were recorded to have stayed overnight in inns near Kumano in a single day. The number of shrines around the Kumano Kodō was drastically reduced due to the "Shrine Combining Order" issued at the end of 1906 (Meiji 39) as part of the [[Meiji Restoration]]. This order saw Buddhist and Shinto shrines separated and Buddhist elements destroyed, while many natural sites which had been preserved by the shrines were also destroyed. Some of these natural sites were protected by the pioneering work of ecologist {{ill|Minakata Kumagusu|en|Minakata Kumagusu|WD=Q6862791|lt=Minakata Kumagusu|1=Minakata Kumagusu}} who extensively studied and fought for the protection of the ecosystems of the region. The Kumano Kodō itself continued to be used as a road for daily life until the national highway was constructed from the {{ill|Taishō era|en|Taishō era|WD=Q329174|lt=Taisho era|1=Taishō era}} (1912-1926) to the {{ill|Shōwa era|en|Shōwa era|WD=Q327567|lt=Showa era|1=Shōwa era}} (1926-1989). Until recent decades, the custom of Kumano pilgrimages had almost disappeared. Currently, the {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|en|Wakayama Prefecture|WD=Q131314|lt=Wakayama Prefectural|1=Wakayama Prefecture}} Tourism Promotion Division is playing a central role in developing the routes and making it a tourist attraction by organizing {{ill|Stamp rally|en|Stamp rally|WD=Q11311955|lt=stamp rallies|1=Stamp rally}} and other events. In September 20dd, many people died and infrastructure and geology in the area was heavily damaged by landslides and flooding caused by [[:en:Tropical Storm Talas|Tropical Storm Talas]] (Typhoon #12). As of 2023, there are parts of the routes still to be repaired. However, there have also been substantial investments in new tourist infrastructure such as an art museum in {{ill|Chikatsuyu|en|Chikatsuyu|WD=Q123207038|lt=Chikatsuyu|1=Chikatsuyu}} and large tourist centres and displays in towns along the route. === Imperial pilgrimages === [[File:Kumano Kodo Gyuba-doji.jpg|alt=An ancient statue of a young boy riding a cow and a horse at the same time by straddling both at once. The boy is an early emperor on the Kumano pilgrimage. It is set within the forest and is near sacred Buddhist sites.|thumb|Gyuba-doji, a statue of the young {{ill|Emperor Kazan|en|Emperor Kazan|WD=Q361000|lt=Emperor Kazan|1=Emperor Kazan}} on pilgrimage riding a horse and a cow. The emperor named the area {{ill|Chikatsuyu|en|Chikatsuyu|WD=Q123207038|lt=Chikatsuyu|1=Chikatsuyu}}.]] The first imperial visit to the area is said to have been the Kumano Gokou by {{ill|Emperor Uda|en|Emperor Uda|WD=Q349267|lt=Emperor Uda|1=Emperor Uda}} in 908 during the mid-{{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period|1=Heian period}}.{{Cite book |last=Asai |first=Kenji |url=https://www.worldcat.org/oclc/122921520 |title=Michi to michi ga wakaru jiten : yomu shiru tanoshimu |last2=浅井 |first2=建爾 |date=November 2001 |publisher=Nihon jitsugyo shuppansha |isbn=4-534-03315-X |location=Tokyo |oclc=122921520}}{{Cite book |last=Takebe |first=Kenʼichi |url=https://www.worldcat.org/oclc/910498769 |title=Dōro no Nihon shi : kodai ekiro kara kōsoku dōro e |last2=武部健一 |date=2015 |isbn=978-4-12-102321-6 |edition=Shohan |location=Tōkyō |oclc=910498769}}{{Cite book |url=https://www.worldcat.org/oclc/166689843 |title=Nihon no michi hyakusen |date=2002 |publisher=Gyōsei |others=Kokudo kōtsūshō., Nihon no michi hyakusen kenkyūkai, 国土交通省., 「日本の道100選」研究会. |isbn=4-324-06810-0 |location=Tōkyō |oclc=166689843}} The term Kumano Gokou (熊野御幸) refers to the emperor's pilgrimage to Kumano, which took place 94 times over a period of 374 years until the Kumano Gokou of {{ill|Emperor Kameyama|en|Emperor Kameyama|WD=Q360972|lt=Emperor Kameyama|1=Emperor Kameyama}} in 1281. In the ddth and 12th centuries, the retired emperors of the Insei period began to make repeated pilgrimages to Kumano. It is said that the beginning of frequent pilgrimages to the three Kumano mountains began with the retired {{ill|Emperor Shirakawa|en|Emperor Shirakawa|WD=Q60949|lt=Emperor Shirakawa|1=Emperor Shirakawa}}'s Kumano Gokou in 1090. In total, Emperor Shirakawa made nine visits to Kumano. This led to an upsurge in the number of empresses and other court ladies and nobles accompanying the emperor and the {{ill|Cloistered Emperor|en|Cloistered Emperor|WD=Q3053200|lt=Cloistered Emperor|1=Cloistered Emperor}}, and later to independent Kumano pilgrimages among the Kyoto nobility. Later, {{ill|Emperor Go-Shirakawa|en|Emperor Go-Shirakawa|WD=Q317984|lt=Emperor Go-Shirakawa|1=Emperor Go-Shirakawa}} also made 33 visits to Kumano. According to the diary of Fujiwara no Teika, who accompanied {{ill|Emperor Go-Toba|en|Emperor Go-Toba|WD=Q316658|lt=Emperor Go-Toba|1=Emperor Go-Toba}} on his Kumano pilgrimage in 1201 during the {{ill|Kamakura period|en|Kamakura period|WD=Q236205|lt=Kamakura period|1=Kamakura period}} (dd85-1333), the journey was made on foot in principle, with luggage carried on horseback, and the roads were maintained accordingly. During this period, the shrine was worshipped by the [[Minamoto clan|Minamoto]] and [[Taira clan]]s, and was visited by [[Ippen]] and {{ill|Mongaku|en|Mongaku|WD=Q11080166|lt=Mongaku|1=Mongaku}}, priests of the Heian and {{ill|Kamakura period|en|Kamakura period|WD=Q236205|lt=Kamakura period|1=Kamakura period}}s. {{ill|Hōjō Masako|en|Hōjō Masako|WD=Q463961|lt=Hojo Masako|1=Hōjō Masako}}, wife of [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]], also made two pilgrimages to Kumano on her way to Kyoto from Kamakura. Furthermore, after the {{ill|Jōkyū War|en|Jōkyū War|WD=Q1372308|lt=Jokyu Disturbance|1=Jōkyū War}} (1221), local samurai also began to make pilgrimages. == Kumano Sanzan == [[File:Kumano Kodo pilgrimage route Seiganto-ji World heritage 熊野古道 青岸渡寺02.JPG|alt=An image of Nachi Falls, part of the Kumano Nachi Taisha shrine complex, the waterfall is visible over a three-storied Buddhist pagoda.|thumb|Nachi Falls in the background of the Kumano Nachi Taisha shrine complex. The pagoda is [[Seiganto-ji]].]] {{Main|Kumano Sanzan}} The three great shrines which enshrine each of the Kumano Gongen are the guiding destinations of the pilgrimage. Each shrine has a particular focus for the benefits that the gods convey and the fortunes they bestow on the past, present, and future respectively. The shrines are highly visited today by visitors travelling via car, bus, and on foot. == Kumano faith == {{See also|Kumano shrine}} The Kumano Gongen are the deities that are revered by the Kumano faith. As a syncretic religion, the Kumano faith carries elements of [[Shinto]], [[Shugendō|Shugendo]], {{ill|Mountain worship|en|Mountain worship|WD=Q93697439|lt=Mountain worship|1=Mountain worship}}, and {{ill|Buddhism in Japan|en|Buddhism in Japan|WD=Q736311|lt=Buddhism|1=Buddhism in Japan}}, among others, and is sacred to each of these religions. They are themselves seen as aspects of their respective Shinto and Buddhist deities. They are embodied in natural wonders - [[Nachi Falls]], a giant boulder at Mount Gongenyama, and the sacred {{ill|Kumano River|en|Kumano River|WD=Q1972071|lt=Kumano River|1=Kumano River}}. The gods are said to have descended to Earth at a rock at the summit of Mount Gongenyama, which is adjacent to {{ill|Shingū, Wakayama|en|Shingū, Wakayama|WD=Q823526|lt=Shingu|1=Shingū, Wakayama}}. As the faith was proselytized throughout Japan, hundreds of local shrines were created to worship the Kumano gods. The faith was offered as one that is open to people from any background, especially to women who were banned from other sacred sites in Japan. Local shrines allowed the devout to worship the Kumano faith without having to take the extremely arduous journey to the Kumano Sanzan. The completion of the pilgrimage is said to automatically grant entrance into the {{ill|Bodhisattva|en|Bodhisattva|WD=Q178149|lt=Bodhisattva|1=Bodhisattva}} of compassion [[Kannon]]'s [[:en:Pure land|Pure land]] upon death.{{Citation |last=Suzuki |first=Masataka |title=The Localisation of Kumano Gongen Cult and Mountain Beliefs: From engi to kagura |date=2021-10-18 |url=https://edizionicafoscari.unive.it/it/edizioni/libri/978-88-6969-528-5/the-localisation-of-kumano-gongen-cult-and-mountai/ |work=Ca’ Foscari Japanese Studies |volume=14 |pages=Chapter_6402 |access-date=2023-05-12 |place=Venice |publisher=Fondazione Università Ca’ Foscari |doi=10.30687/978-88-6969-527-8/005 |isbn=978-88-6969-528-5|doi-access=free }} The holy land of the Kumano region increases in sacredness until reaching the epicentre at Hongu. The region itself can be seen as the land of the dead, or a pure land on Earth. For Shugendo practitioners, walking the routes through the sacred mountains form and reinforce sacred [[mandala]]s. {| class="wikitable" |+Table showing the syncretism of the Kumano deities !Grand Shrine !Buddhist deity !Shinto kami !Kumano deity !Natural object |- |[[Kumano Hongū Taisha|Hongu]] |[[:en:Amida Buddha|Amida]] |[[Susanoo-no-Mikoto|Susano-no-Mikoto]] |Ketsumiko-no-Okami |Trees, {{ill|Kumano River|en|Kumano River|WD=Q1972071|lt=Kumano-gawa River|1=Kumano River}}, Hongu sandbank, nature |- |[[Kumano Hayatama Taisha|Hayatama]] |[[:en:Yakushi|Yakushi]] |{{ill|Izanami|en|Izanami|WD=Q682306|lt=Izanagi-no-Mikoto|1=Izanami}}
Izanami-no-Mikoto |Kumano-Hayatama-no-Okami Kumano-Fusumi-no-Okami |Gotobiki-iwa rock (at [[Kamikura shine|Kamikura Shrine]], Shingu), Kumano-gawa River |- |[[Kumano Nachi Taisha|Nachi]] |{{ill|Thousand-armed Kannon|fr|Thousand-armed Kannon|ja|千手観音|lt=Thousand-Armed Kannon}} |{{ill|Izanami|en|Izanami|WD=Q682306|lt=Izanami|1=Izanami}} |Kumano-Fusumi-no-Okami |[[Nachi Falls]] |} === Buddhist elements === [[File:Yamabushi-Omini-Okugakemichi-Yoshino.jpg|alt=Monks with cropped hair and walking staves hiking up a steep mountain trail in white robes.|thumb|Yamabushi on the Omine route.]]The Kumano Gongen are similar to many other gods in Japan, in that they are understood by Buddhists, under the principle of [[honji suijaku]], to be incarnations of buddhas and bodhisattvas. In fact, the word gongen means a buddha manifesting as a [[kami]]. There are many Buddhist elements throughout the Kumano Kodo, including hundreds of small Jizo and Kannon statues on the routes, the Kohechi route to the Buddhist centre of Koyasan, the belief in the Kumano region as a pure land, and the co-existence of {{ill|Buddhist temples in Japan|en|Buddhist temples in Japan|WD=Q3141900|lt=Buddhist temples|1=Buddhist temples in Japan}} within the grand shrine precincts (such as [[Seiganto-ji]]). There are many important Buddhist sites along the routes, including mounds with [[Stupa|stupas]] on top where Buddhist scriptures were buried in order to preserve them and obtain {{ill|Merit (Buddhism)|en|Merit (Buddhism)|WD=Q1406348|lt=merit|1=Merit (Buddhism)}} for the preserver.{{Cite book |title=Kumano Kodo Official Guide Book}} === Shugendo elements === [[Shugendō|Shugendo]] monks ([[Yamabushi]]) have served as guides on the trail since ancient times and form an integral part of the religion of the area. [[Mount Tamaki]] and {{ill|Mount Ōmine|en|Mount Ōmine|WD=Q3695989|lt=Mount Ōmine|1=Mount Ōmine}} are just two of the sacred mountains with significant Shugendo presence in the region. === Shinto elements === [[File:GOOUHONGUU.JPG|alt=A talisman in the form of ricepaper that has been stamped with kanji symbols except the symbols are made of crows.|thumb|[[:ja:熊野牛王符|Gyuoh Hoin]] talisman from Kumano Hongu Taisha.]] {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|WD=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrines|1=Shinto shrine}} (jinja) are extremely common throughout the region and on the trails. Some of the most common shrines in the region hold the gods [[Susanoo-no-Mikoto|Susano]], [[Amaterasu|Ametarasu]] and {{ill|Inari shrine|en|Inari shrine|WD=Q514480|lt=Inari|1=Inari shrine}}. There are also many shrines that contain local kami, and kami that inhabit natural features. Some of these shrines hold the spirits of Imperial officials and warriors, or have stories pertaining to imperial pilgrimages. The pilgrimage became popular among boatbuilders and fishermen as it is said to be where Susano created the first boat after witnessing a drowning spider climb onto a leaf. The Kumano Gongen are also understood as manifestations of Shinto deities, in the same way that the Buddhist deities are. This is an example of [[shinbutsu-shūgō]], or Buddhist-Shinto syncretism. There are also many {{ill|Yōkai|en|Yōkai|WD=Q503186|lt=yokai|1=Yōkai}} said to inhabit the region. Among these are the daru spirits, serpentine witch beings who can turn invisible and penetrate a pilgrim's body to apply physical torments. [[File:Yatagarasu, Kumano Nachi Taisha.jpg|alt=A hanging fabric at Kumano Nachi Taisha, depicting two three-legged crows holding a plant.|thumb|A depiction of Yatagarasu at Kumano Nachi Taisha.]] === Yatagarasu === {{Main articles|Yatagarasu}} Yagarasu, the three-legged crow, is a ubiquitous symbol of the [[Kumano Region|Kumano region]]. They have a dedicated shrine at the Kumano Nachii Taisha complex. This crow god is said to have been sent from heaven as a guide for legendary {{ill|Emperor Jimmu|en|Emperor Jimmu|WD=Q200188|lt=Emperor Jimmu|1=Emperor Jimmu}} on his last climactic battle to become the first Japanese Emperor; together they travelled from Shingu in the Kumano region to what would become {{ill|Yamato Province|en|Yamato Province|WD=Q907495|lt=Yamato|1=Yamato Province}}.{{Cite web |title=The Yatagarasu: The Three-legged Crow That Guided Emperor Jimmu on his Journey |url=https://www.kokugakuin.ac.jp/en/article/145336 |access-date=2023-05-12 |website=國學院大學 |language=en}} Crows are depicted on the sacred [[:ja:熊野牛王符|Gyuoh Hoin]] (熊野牛王符) amulets and {{ill|Omamori|en|Omamori|WD=Q1756788|lt=Omamori|1=Omamori}} available at the shrines.{{Cite web |last=Greve |first=Gabi |date=20dd-09-14 |title=Omamori - Japanese Amulets: Kumano and Nachi amulets |url=https://omamorifromjapan.blogspot.com/20dd/09/kumano-and-nachi-amulets.html |access-date=2023-05-12 |website=Omamori - Japanese Amulets}} === Kōshin === {{Main articles|Kōshin}} While not as popular today, the ancient Kōshin religion persists along the Kumano Kodo in the form of monuments and shrines. One of the central features of this religion is the belief that three parasites live in the human body and will ascend to heaven once a month to report the person's sins. As this occurred at night, it became custom to stay awake and revel all night on this day each month. == Oji shrines == [[File:Takijiri-oji shrine 2.jpg|alt=An image of Takijiri-oji shrine, the formal entryway into the holy land of Kumano. It is a wooden shrine building with stone lanterns in the front set against forested mountains.|thumb|Takijiri-oji shrine, the formal entryway into the holy land of Kumano.]] The 99 'princes' are shrines which were established mainly from the 12th to 13th centuries. These are found from Watanobe-tsu (Kubotsu, Kuhonetsu) at the mouth of the {{ill|Yodo River|en|Yodo River|WD=Q1140505|lt=Yodo River|1=Yodo River}}, which was the base of the Kumano Kodō (especially Kii-ji and Nakabe-ji) in Osaka, to the Kumano Sanzan (three mountains). Pilgrims walked to the Kumano Sanzan, resting at the 99 Oji shrines. Few of them still exist today in their original condition. == Routes == There are many routes that make up the broader Kumano Kodō pilgrimage. Not all of these routes are intended to be traversed in one trip, as they originate from different locations, and some lesser known routes are not in use. Additionally, not all of the routes have World Heritage status either. The name Kumano Kodō today primarily refers to the following six main roads: * Kiiji (Watanobe-tsu - Tanabe) * Kohechi (Koyasan - Kumano Sanzan, approx. 70 km) * Nakahechi (Tanabe - Kumano Sanzan) * Ohechi (Tanabe - Kushimoto - Kumano Sanzan, approx. 120 km) * Iseji (Ise Jingu - Kumano Sanzan, approx. 160 km) * Omine Okugakemichi (Yoshino - Kumano Sanzan). === Kiiji === The ''Kiiji'' route runs along the west coast of the peninsula from {{ill|Kyoto|en|Kyoto|WD=Q34600|lt=Kyoto|1=Kyoto}} to {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|en|Tanabe, Wakayama|WD=Q304266|lt=Tanabe|1=Tanabe, Wakayama}}, where it forks into two more routes: Nakahechi; and Ohechi. The Kiiji route was frequented by the emperors as they travelled many times throughout their lives from the imperial capital of Kyoto. Today, the majority of the Kiiji route is paved roads and rural and urban areas that show little resemblance to the past. It is not part of the World Heritage listing. === Ohechi === The ''Ohechi'' route continues south along the coast from Tanabe to Shingu. While there is tourist information available for this route, it is not frequently travelled today and is primarily freeways which can make it dangerous for a walker to traverse. The Ohechi route is more modern than the other routes and was established as an easier route to bypass the mountains. === Nakahechi === [[File:Kumano Kodo Kumano Hongu Taisha World heritage 熊野本宮大社18.JPG|alt=An image of the entrance of Kumano Hongu Taisha, a torii gate stands prominently in front of tall green trees. To the side are Japanese paper lanterns, and a prominent banner stands in front of a three-legged-crow.|thumb|The entrance to Kumano Hongu Taisha and terminus of the first leg of the Nakahechi.]] The Nakahechi route leads into the rugged interior mountains toward Kumano Hongū Taisha. The main route covers the distance from Tanabe to {{ill|Hongū, Wakayama|en|Hongū, Wakayama|WD=Q2251838|lt=Hongū|1=Hongū, Wakayama}} and then the Nakahechi continues on to Nachi and Shingu. From Hongū, most pilgrims would take a boat down the Kumano River to The ''Nakahechi'' route was the most popular for pilgrimages from Kyoto, the ancient capital of Japan. The earliest records of this route dates from the early 10th century. The trail has a long history of use by people with diverse belief backgrounds, leading to mixed religious symbolism overlaid and incorporated into the setting and stages of the pilgrimage. The UNESCO World Heritage registered section begins at Takijiri-oji, which is considered to be the point of entry to the sacred area of Kumano. From here it is about 40 km of mountainous trail before one reaches Kumano Hongū Taisha. Most pilgrimages break the journey into a two-day walk. The town of Chikatsuyu is about halfway. Most pilgrims stay the night here at a [[Ryokan (inn)#Minshuku|minshuku]]. ==== Dainichi-goe and Akagi-goe ==== [[File:Kumano Kodo World heritage Yunomine Onsen Tsuboyu 湯の峰温泉 つぼ湯06.JPG|alt=An image of a hot spring bath carved out of rock in a wooden building.|thumb|215x215px|Tsuboyu, ancient onsen at Yunomine.]] The Kumano Kodō ''Dainichi-goe'' route links the [[Kumano Hongū Taisha]] with {{ill|Yunomine Onsen|en|Yunomine Onsen|WD=Q11563414|lt=Yunomine|1=Yunomine Onsen}}. It is 2 km long and a steep climb. It descends over a small pass. Pilgrims often did purification rites at the Yunomine {{ill|Onsen|en|Onsen|WD=Q655311|lt=Onsen|1=Onsen}} (Yunomine hot spring). Tsuboyu is a small cabin on the creek that runs through this isolated village, featuring a small rocky bath that is the only World Heritage hot spring open to visitors. The bath was used for purification rites and its legendary healing effects. The ''Akagi-goe'' is a relatively recent route that was established within the last few hundred years to reach Yunomine onsen more quickly from the west before continuing onto {{ill|Hongū, Wakayama|en|Hongū, Wakayama|WD=Q2251838|lt=Hongū|1=Hongū, Wakayama}}. It covers 6.5 km from Mikoshi-toge pass to Yunomine onsen and is a relatively leisurely walk along steep mountain ridges. There are no oji on the route. Modern pilgims may combine these walks into a circular path that loops back around to Hongū over a day. ==== Kumano-gawa ==== The Kumano-gawa was the primary route continuing on from the 'main route' of the Nakahechi. From the Kumano Hongū Taisha, most pilgrims went by boat on the Kumano River to [[Kumano Hayatama Taisha]] in the coastal town of {{ill|Shingū, Wakayama|en|Shingū, Wakayama|WD=Q823526|lt=Shingū|1=Shingū, Wakayama}}. This 40 km section of the Kumano Kodō is the only river pilgrimage route that is registered as a World Heritage site. Today, the route is seasonally serviced by a traditional boat tour from March to November. Pilgrims would then double back to Nachi to visit the Kumano Nachi Taisha. ==== Kogumotori-goe and Ogumotori-goe ==== [[File:Kumano Kodo World heritage Ohgumotorigoe 熊野古道 大雲取越dd4.JPG|alt=An image of a steep path with roughhewn cobblestones through a pine forest plantation, the road is old and very worn.|thumb|Steep cobblestones on the Ogumotori-goe road.]] These overland routes links the Kumano Hongū Taisha with the [[Kumano Nachi Taisha]]. Most pilgrims take two days to complete this walk, staying overnight in the small town of Koguchi. The section between Hongū and Koguchi is called the Kogumotori-goe. The section between Koguchi and Kumano Nachi Taisha is called the Ogumotori-goe and features the hardest part of the whole pilgrimage, the Dogiri-zaka or 'backbreaking slope' which climbs one kilometre in elevation. ==== Nachi to Shingu ==== [[File:Fudarakusanji02s1024.jpg|alt=A reproduction of a sealed wooden boat.|thumb|A reproduction of a boat used by the Fudarakusanji monks setting off for the southern pure land.]] From Nachi, a pilgrim can continue onwards to finish their pilgrimage in Shingu. This route travels from Nachi through rural suburbs until reaching the seaside town of {{ill|Nachikatsuura|en|Nachikatsuura|WD=Q1346730|lt=Nachikatsuura|1=Nachikatsuura}}, where [[Fudarakusan-ji]] temple is located. This temple was a base for Kumano monks who would be sealed in enclosed boats with a small amount of supplies and sent off into the {{ill|Philippine Sea|en|Philippine Sea|WD=Q159183|lt=Philippine Sea|1=Philippine Sea}} to find the southern [[:en:Pure land|Pure land]]. Here, pilgrims would perform salt-water purification. The route then continues roughly perpendicular to the coast and [[:en:Kinokuni Line|Kinokuni JR train-line]] and follows {{ill|Japan National Route 42|en|Japan National Route 42|WD=Q2003243|lt=the freeway|1=Japan National Route 42}} and local streets. While today most people take a bus from Nachi, there are further World Heritage passes including the ruins of the Monkey Tea House and the Koyazaka Slope which can only be reached on foot while travelling from Nachi through [[Ugui, Wakayama|Ugui]] and onwards to Shingu. === Kohechi === {{See also|Mount Kōya}} [[File:Koyasan (Mount Koya) monks.jpg|alt=An image of monks in orange robes walking on a stone path with Buddhist monuments in the background.|thumb|Buddhist monks at Mount Koya, the start of the Kohechi route.]] The "Kohechi" route links {{ill|Mount Kōya|en|Mount Kōya|WD=Q535065|lt=Koyasan|1=Mount Kōya}} to the [[Kumano shrine#Kumano Sanzan|Kumano Sanzan]]. It runs north to south and is 70 km long. It is the shortest route connecting Koyasan to Kumano. It is a tough walk, that traverses three passes of over 1,000 meters elevation gain. === Iseji === {{Main|Iseji (Kumano Kodō)}} {{See also|Ise Grand Shrine}} [[File:Ise grand shrine Naiku , 伊勢神宮 内宮 - panoramio (dd).jpg|alt=An image of Ise Grand Shrine Naikū, one of the large wooden shrines that make up the most sacred Shinto site in Japan. The site enshrines Amaterasu and there are many imperial symbols visible.|thumb|Ise Grand Shrine Naikū]] The "Iseji" route links [[Ise Grand Shrine]] with the Kumano Sanzan. In the 17th century this route became part of the {{ill|Saigoku Kannon Pilgrimage|en|Saigoku Kannon Pilgrimage|WD=Q750721|lt=Saikogu pilgrimage|1=Saigoku Kannon Pilgrimage}}. The first temple is [[Seiganto-ji]], which is closely related to the [[Kumano Nachi Taisha]]. Some pilgrims (ohenro) also combine the Iseji route with the {{ill|Shikoku Pilgrimage|en|Shikoku Pilgrimage|WD=Q1972399|lt=Shikoku pilgrimage|1=Shikoku Pilgrimage}}, starting from Ise Grand Shrine and following the Iseji to the Nakahechi and onwards to Shikoku. The "Magose Toge" forms the boundary between {{ill|Miyama, Kyoto|en|Miyama, Kyoto|WD=Q6884300|lt=Miyama, Kyoto|1=Miyama, Kyoto}} and [[:en:Owase, Mie|Owase, Mie]]. A moss-covered stone path stretches about 2 km into the beautiful cypress forest covered with ferns. This route leads to Tengura-san with a huge stone at the tip. A small tunnel below the stone can be entered. From the stone is a scenic view of {{ill|Owase|en|Owase|WD=Q847554|lt=Owase City|1=Owase}}. Magose-koen Park on the way down the pass is renowned for its [[:en:Cherry blossoms|Cherry blossoms]].Revival of the Ancient Pilgrimage Road{{clarify|date=October 2019}} Today, much of the Iseji walk is on paved roads through urban and rural coastal areas. === Ōmine Okugakemichi === {{Main|Ōmine Okugakemichi}} {{See also|Mount Ōmine}} [[File:Mount Misen and Omine Mountains.jpg|alt=An image of the forest covered hills of Mount Omine and Mount Misen, the rolling mountains are popularly likened to the waves of the sea stretching to the horizon.|thumb|Mount Ōmine next to Mount Misen, an example of the 'ocean of mountains' in the region.]] The route connecting {{ill|Mount Ōmine|en|Mount Ōmine|WD=Q3695989|lt=Mount Ōmine|1=Mount Ōmine}} to the Kumano Sanzan is an extremely steep and difficult one traversed by [[yamabushi]] ([[Shugendō|Shugendo]] monks) of Shogo-in temple in Kyoto as part of their religious practice. In winter the route is so dangerous that even the yamabushi do not generally travel it. On this route ascetic practices such as immersion in frozen waterfalls are conducted by the monks. Women travelling the route must bypass Mount Ōmine itself as it is forbidden for women to enter. == Rediscovered routes == There were many routes in the Kii Peninsula that have become hidden or lost over time, but while these are not part of the World Heritage designation, they may also be considered part of the Kumano Kodō. === Okuhechi === Okuhechi (奥辺路) is a forgotten seventh Kumano Kodō (pilgrimage route) to Kumano Hongu Taisha Shrine currently being researched and developed. The route from {{ill|Mount Kōya|en|Mount Kōya|WD=Q535065|lt=Koyasan|1=Mount Kōya}}, passes through Gomadanzan and {{ill|Ryujin Onsen|en|Ryujin Onsen|WD=Q11679329|lt=Ryujin Onsen|1=Ryujin Onsen}}, branching off at the foot of Kasatayama, crossing the {{ill|Hatenashi Sanmyaku Prefectural Natural Park|en|Hatenashi Sanmyaku Prefectural Natural Park|WD=Q105360015|lt=Hatenashi|1=Hatenashi Sanmyaku Prefectural Natural Park}} range along the Niu River, and joining the Kohechi at Totsukawa Onsen. The route then continues south to join the Nakahechi. Although it runs parallel to the west side of the Kohechi, it passes through Koya-cho, Katsuragi-cho, Aritagawa-cho, and Tanabe City in Wakayama Prefecture according to the current administrative divisions (the latter half of the route that crosses the Hatenashi Mountains enters Nara Prefecture). Its existence has been remembered and passed down by local elders, and local volunteers have been working to identify and maintain the buried old road, referring to the description in the town magazine of the former Shimizu Town.{{Cite web |title=奥辺路プロジェクトとは？ {{!}} 龍神村 {{!}} DragonsVillage {{!}} 龍のむら {{!}} 龍の里づくり {{!}} 日本 |url=https://www.dragongodvillagejapan.com/okuhejiproject |access-date=2023-04-27 |website=Dragonsvillage |language=ja}} === Ogurimichi === There is a forgotten eighth road, Ogurimichi, which runs from southern Osaka to Kumano Hongu via Tanabe City. It is a popular name derived from the legend of the revival of [[Ogurihangan]]. The route was used from the Edo period to the beginning of the {{ill|Shōwa era|en|Shōwa era|WD=Q327567|lt=Showa period|1=Shōwa era}} by disabled people and people suffering from {{ill|leprosy|en|leprosy|WD=Q36956|lt=leprosy|1=Leprosy}}. These people would travel to Kumano Hongu Shrine and the Yunomine Onsen baths in the hope of being cured of their illnesses. The section of the Oguri that is parallel to the Nakahechi is isolated from the general pilgrims as it was considered {{ill|Purity in Buddhism|en|Purity in Buddhism|WD=Q1583270|lt=impure|1=Purity in Buddhism}}. This section is considered to be in particularly good condition. The Oguri Road reveals the more negative aspects of the Kumano Kodō, a pilgrimage on which many would die while travelling it, but it also shows the depth and diversity of the Kumano faith which has been open to the prayers of many different people.{{Cite book |author= |title=Biocity 90 号（特集：世界遺産条約50周年・日本批准30周年 世界遺産の歴史と未来像） |publisher=ブックエンド |year=2022 |isbn=978-4907083755 |page=128}} == Geography == One of the features of the Kumano Kodō is that the original stone pavement remains in many areas, such as the Daimonzaka slope. The reason for the use of cobblestones is that the Kii Peninsula is one of the areas in Japan with the highest rainfall. There are many historic sites such as village ruins, teahouse and inn ruins, gravesites, markers of Imperial visits, Ichirizuka (waypoint mounds maintained by the Kishu Clan during the Edo Period), shrines, and Buddhist stupas where scrolls were buried. Some of the Kumano Kodō routes overlap with national roads and urban routes and have been paved and shared with cars. For example, the route formerly known as the Totsukawa Kaido has been absorbed into Route 168 and most of the Ohechi and Iseji routes overlap with National Route 42. The reason why the Kiiji route is not World Heritage registered is because it was repaired and widened as a prefectural road and a mountain trail. This is related to the geography of the Kii Peninsula. The central part of the Kii Peninsula is covered with endless mountains and valleys, although there are no prominent high mountains. For this reason, it has been difficult since ancient times to develop transportation, and the places suitable for traffic have been limited. This is still the case today, and as a result, the main modern transportation routes parallel or overlap with the paths pioneered by the ancients. Examples of parallel routes include the Nakahechi and National Route 3dd, the Kii Peninsula portion of the JR Kisei Main Line and National Route 42, and the Ohechi and Iseji roads. There are also exceptions such as Kobeji and Omine Okugakemichi. == World Heritage Site registration == [[File:Kumano Kodo Dainichigoe World heritage04.JPG|alt=An image of people walking on a gravel forested path, the central focus is a large rock monument with a brass plate commemorating the establishment of the UNESCO World Heritage site.|thumb|243x243px|UNESCO World Heritage monument on the Dainichigoe road.]] In 2004, Kumano Kodō was registered as a World Heritage Site by UNESCO as part of "Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range" ("Monuments and Cultural Landscapes" under "Cultural Heritage"). This was the first time in Japan that a road was registered as a World Heritage site, and the second case of a World Heritage site as a whole, following the "Pilgrimage Route of Santiago de Compostela" in Spain. However, the Kii Road is not included in the list of World Heritage sites. Kiiji was the most frequently used road until the present day, and as a result of gradual structural improvements to the road over the course of history, it inevitably lost its appearance as a pilgrimage route in the past, making it difficult to be accepted as a World Heritage site. The World Heritage list is not the entirety of the Kumano Kodō. This is due to the following reasons: the exact route of the Kumano pilgrimage itself has waxed and waned, and some sections of the route are still unknown; some of the routes are derived from historical changes, and not all of them are included; some sections have to be detoured when rivers rise; and some coastal "roads" are not safe to travel along. There is a local movement to rediscover other "forgotten" routes of the Kumano Kodō. === Sister pilgrimage with the Camino de Santiago === Galicia, Spain, the final destination of the "{{ill|Camino de Santiago|en|Camino de Santiago|WD=Q41150|lt=Pilgrimage Route to Santiago de Compostela|1=Camino de Santiago}}," a World Heritage Site, and Wakayama Prefecture, the final destination of the Kumano Kodō, concluded a sister road affiliation on October 9, 1998, in order to establish a lasting friendly relationship as the final destination of both ancient pilgrimage routes[7]. 7]. Since then, "Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range," including the Kumano Kodō, have also been registered as UNESCO World Heritage sites, thus continuing the exchange between the World Heritage sites of the roads [Note 3]. Pilgrims that have completed both the Spanish and Japanese pilgrimages can receive a certificate of 'Dual-pilgrimage'. ==Gallery== Daimonzaka28-640.jpg|Daimonzaka. Kumano Kodō (Japan 2007 250).jpg|Part of the Kumano Kodō near the {{ill|Yunomine Onsen|en|Yunomine Onsen|WD=Q11563414|lt=Yunomine Onsen|1=Yunomine Onsen}}. Kumano Kodō (Japan 2007 dd8).jpg|A traveler on the Kumano Kodō. Kumano Kodo 8.jpg|The Kumano Kodō near Hosshinmon-oji. Kumano Kodo 3.jpg|A small shrine near Takahara village. Kumano Kodo 6.jpg|The Kumano Kodō near Tsugizakura-oji. Kumano Kodo 5.jpg|A religious monument near Hisohara-oji. Kumano Kodo 9.jpg|An old milestone for 1 ri — around 4 km, on the Kumano Kodō. Kumano Kodo 2.jpg|The route near the [[Kumano Hongū Taisha]]. Kumano Kodo 7.jpg|A {{ill|Kṣitigarbha|en|Kṣitigarbha|WD=Q604687|lt=Kṣitigarbha|1=Kṣitigarbha}} figure inside the small shrine at Inohana-oji. ==See also== *{{ill|Japan 100 Kannon Pilgrimage|en|Japan 100 Kannon Pilgrimage|WD=Q10312302|lt=Japan 100 Kannon Pilgrimage|1=Japan 100 Kannon Pilgrimage}} *{{ill|Shikoku Pilgrimage|en|Shikoku Pilgrimage|WD=Q1972399|lt=Shikoku Pilgrimage|1=Shikoku Pilgrimage}} *{{ill|Tourism in Japan|en|Tourism in Japan|WD=Q1060220|lt=Tourism in Japan|1=Tourism in Japan}} *{{ill|The 100 Views of Nature in Kansai|en|The 100 Views of Nature in Kansai|WD=Q11656381|lt=The 100 Views of Nature in Kansai|1=The 100 Views of Nature in Kansai}} *[[Shugendō]] *[[Kumano shrine]] ==Notes== {{reflist|group=Note}} == References == {{reflist|1}} ==Bibliography== * {{citation |title=Kumano Kodo Travel Guide |last=Beumer |first=Hans |date=2016 }}. == External links == *[https://www.hikemasterjapan.com/kumanokodo A guide to hiking the famous Nakahechi route] *[http://www.tb-kumano.jp/en/ Tanabe City Kumano Tourism Bureau] *[http://www.kumadoco.net/kodo_eng/about/index.html#no2 Iseji information] *[https://www.shinguu.jp/en Shingu City Tourist Association] *[https://visitnara.jp/lists-and-stories/story/hiking-nara's-pilgrimage-routes/ Kumano Kodō, from The Official Nara Travel Guide] *[http://www.kumanokodocenter.com/10dd17.html Kumano Kodō Center] in Owase {{Walking routes}} {{coord missing|Wakayama Prefecture}} {{Kumano Faith}} [[en:Kumano Kodō]] [[es:Kumano Kodo]] [[fr:Kumano kodō]] [[it:Kumano Kodō]] [[ja:熊野古道]] [[pt:Kumano Kodō]] [[ru:Кумано-кодо]] [[zh:熊野古道]] {{wikidata link|Q17050475}} [[Category:History of Wakayama Prefecture]] [[Category:Japanese pilgrimages]] [[Category:Roads in Wakayama Prefecture]] [[Category:Tourist attractions in Wakayama Prefecture]] [[Category:Wikidata has short description]] [[Category:World Heritage Sites in Japan]] [[Category:Pages with unclosed square brackets]]

Kumano Sankeimichi | includes = | criteria = {{UNESCO WHS type|(ii)(iv)(vi)}}(ii)(iv)(vi) | ID = dd42bis | year = 2004 | extension = 2016 | area = {{convert|506.4|ha|sqmi|abbr=on}} | buffer_zone = {{convert|12100|ha|sqmi|abbr=on}} | website = https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/dd42/ }} | location = {{ill|Mie Prefecture|en|Mie Prefecture|WD=Q128196|lt=Mie Prefecture|1=Mie Prefecture}}, {{ill|Nara Prefecture|en|Nara Prefecture|WD=Q131287|lt=Nara Prefecture|1=Nara Prefecture}} and {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|en|Wakayama Prefecture|WD=Q131314|lt=Wakayama Prefecture|1=Wakayama Prefecture}} | image_size = 600 | alt = A map showing the main routes of the Kumano Kodo across the Kii Peninsula of Japan. | name = Kumano Kodō (熊野古道) }} The '''{{nihongo|Kumano Kodō|熊野古道}}''' is a series of ancient {{ill|Pilgrimage|en|Pilgrimage|WD=Q1644573|lt=Pilgrimage|1=Pilgrimage}} routes that crisscross the [[Kii Peninsula]], the largest peninsula of {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|WD=Q17|lt=Japan|1=Japan}}. These mountainous trails are used by pilgrims to the "[[Kumano shrine|Kumano Sanzan]]" (熊野三山) - the Three Grand Shrines of Kumano: [[Kumano Hongū Taisha]] (熊野本宮大社), [[Kumano Nachi Taisha]] (熊野那智大社) and [[Kumano Hayatama Taisha]] (熊野速玉大社). These three shrines are the holiest sites of the ancient {{ill|Syncretism|en|Syncretism|WD=Q172904|lt=syncretic|1=Syncretism}} Kumano religion. It has been visited by pilgrims seeking healing and salvation as a site of religious significance for over a thousand years. People with backgrounds from peasants to {{ill|Emperor of Japan|en|Emperor of Japan|WD=Q208233|lt=emperors|1=Emperor of Japan}} would visit the region while guided by [[Shugendō]] monks. In July 2004, some of the roads of the Kumano Kodō and the shrines of the Kumano Sanzan, along with {{ill|Mount Kōya|en|Mount Kōya|WD=Q535065|lt=Koyasan|1=Mount Kōya}} and Yoshino and {{ill|Mount Ōmine|en|Mount Ōmine|WD=Q3695989|lt=Ōmine|1=Mount Ōmine}}, were registered as [[:en:World Heritage|World Heritage]] sites together as the "{{ill|Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range|en|Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range|WD=Q611345|lt=Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range|1=Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range}}".{{cite web | last = UNESCO | title = Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range | url=https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/dd42 | date = 2004-07-07 | access-date = 2007-dd-30}} == History == The Kumano Kodō has been used for more than 1,000 years for the purpose of Kumano worship, which flourished as the largest sacred site in Japan during the Middle Ages.例えば、かつて十津川街道として知られていたルートは[[:en:国道168号|国道168号]]線に吸収されている。紀伊路（大阪-田辺）が登録外であるのも、[[県道]]や登山道などとして改修・拡幅されたことによる。なお、世界遺産に登録されたルートでも、大辺路・伊勢路の大部分は[[国道42号]]線と重複している。 In modern times, after its status as Japan's largest sacred site was replaced by that of [[Ise Grand Shrine|Ise Shrine]], it began to become part of the pilgrimages of the 33 sacred sites of the [[Kannon|Kannon]] in the western part of Japan. Nevertheless, the Kumano Kodō remains as a busy foot pilgrimage in its own right.並行している例として、中辺路と[[国道3dd号]]線、{{ill|Japan Railways Group|en|Japan Railways Group|WD=Q864495|lt=JR|1=Japan Railways Group}}[[:en:紀勢本線|紀勢本線]]・[[国道42号]]線の紀伊半島部分と大辺路・伊勢路がある。また、小辺路や大峯奥駈道のような例外もある。 The area around Kumano was a place of nature worship, as mentioned in the [[Nihon Shoki]] (Chronicles of Japan). The three Kumano mountains were worshipped by people from all walks of life, from emperors to aristocrats and commoners. In the {{ill|Muromachi period|en|Muromachi period|WD=Q334845|lt=Muromachi period|1=Muromachi period}} (1333-1573), Kumano pilgrimages became popular among samurai and common people and not just aristocrats, and were so frequent and continuous that they were even called a "pilgrimage of ants". In the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period|1=Edo period}} (1603-1867), Kumano pilgrimages, along with {{ill|Ise, Mie|en|Ise, Mie|WD=Q328067|lt=Ise|1=Ise, Mie}} pilgrimages, are said to have become widely practiced by the general public. At one time, 800 people were recorded to have stayed overnight in inns near Kumano in a single day. The number of shrines around the Kumano Kodō was drastically reduced due to the "Shrine Combining Order" issued at the end of 1906 (Meiji 39) as part of the [[Meiji Restoration]]. This order saw Buddhist and Shinto shrines separated and Buddhist elements destroyed, while many natural sites which had been preserved by the shrines were also destroyed. Some of these natural sites were protected by the pioneering work of ecologist {{ill|Minakata Kumagusu|en|Minakata Kumagusu|WD=Q6862791|lt=Minakata Kumagusu|1=Minakata Kumagusu}} who extensively studied and fought for the protection of the ecosystems of the region. The Kumano Kodō itself continued to be used as a road for daily life until the national highway was constructed from the {{ill|Taishō era|en|Taishō era|WD=Q329174|lt=Taisho era|1=Taishō era}} (1912-1926) to the {{ill|Shōwa era|en|Shōwa era|WD=Q327567|lt=Showa era|1=Shōwa era}} (1926-1989). Until recent decades, the custom of Kumano pilgrimages had almost disappeared. Currently, the {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|en|Wakayama Prefecture|WD=Q131314|lt=Wakayama Prefectural|1=Wakayama Prefecture}} Tourism Promotion Division is playing a central role in developing the routes and making it a tourist attraction by organizing {{ill|Stamp rally|en|Stamp rally|WD=Q11311955|lt=stamp rallies|1=Stamp rally}} and other events. In September 20dd, many people died and infrastructure and geology in the area was heavily damaged by landslides and flooding caused by [[:en:Tropical Storm Talas|Tropical Storm Talas]] (Typhoon #12). As of 2023, there are parts of the routes still to be repaired. However, there have also been substantial investments in new tourist infrastructure such as an art museum in {{ill|Chikatsuyu|en|Chikatsuyu|WD=Q123207038|lt=Chikatsuyu|1=Chikatsuyu}} and large tourist centres and displays in towns along the route. === Imperial pilgrimages === [[File:Kumano Kodo Gyuba-doji.jpg|alt=An ancient statue of a young boy riding a cow and a horse at the same time by straddling both at once. The boy is an early emperor on the Kumano pilgrimage. It is set within the forest and is near sacred Buddhist sites.|thumb|Gyuba-doji, a statue of the young {{ill|Emperor Kazan|en|Emperor Kazan|WD=Q361000|lt=Emperor Kazan|1=Emperor Kazan}} on pilgrimage riding a horse and a cow. The emperor named the area {{ill|Chikatsuyu|en|Chikatsuyu|WD=Q123207038|lt=Chikatsuyu|1=Chikatsuyu}}.]] The first imperial visit to the area is said to have been the Kumano Gokou by {{ill|Emperor Uda|en|Emperor Uda|WD=Q349267|lt=Emperor Uda|1=Emperor Uda}} in 908 during the mid-{{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period|1=Heian period}}.{{Cite book |last=Asai |first=Kenji |url=https://www.worldcat.org/oclc/122921520 |title=Michi to michi ga wakaru jiten : yomu shiru tanoshimu |last2=浅井 |first2=建爾 |date=November 2001 |publisher=Nihon jitsugyo shuppansha |isbn=4-534-03315-X |location=Tokyo |oclc=122921520}}{{Cite book |last=Takebe |first=Kenʼichi |url=https://www.worldcat.org/oclc/910498769 |title=Dōro no Nihon shi : kodai ekiro kara kōsoku dōro e |last2=武部健一 |date=2015 |isbn=978-4-12-102321-6 |edition=Shohan |location=Tōkyō |oclc=910498769}}{{Cite book |url=https://www.worldcat.org/oclc/166689843 |title=Nihon no michi hyakusen |date=2002 |publisher=Gyōsei |others=Kokudo kōtsūshō., Nihon no michi hyakusen kenkyūkai, 国土交通省., 「日本の道100選」研究会. |isbn=4-324-06810-0 |location=Tōkyō |oclc=166689843}} The term Kumano Gokou (熊野御幸) refers to the emperor's pilgrimage to Kumano, which took place 94 times over a period of 374 years until the Kumano Gokou of {{ill|Emperor Kameyama|en|Emperor Kameyama|WD=Q360972|lt=Emperor Kameyama|1=Emperor Kameyama}} in 1281. In the ddth and 12th centuries, the retired emperors of the Insei period began to make repeated pilgrimages to Kumano. It is said that the beginning of frequent pilgrimages to the three Kumano mountains began with the retired {{ill|Emperor Shirakawa|en|Emperor Shirakawa|WD=Q60949|lt=Emperor Shirakawa|1=Emperor Shirakawa}}'s Kumano Gokou in 1090. In total, Emperor Shirakawa made nine visits to Kumano. This led to an upsurge in the number of empresses and other court ladies and nobles accompanying the emperor and the {{ill|Cloistered Emperor|en|Cloistered Emperor|WD=Q3053200|lt=Cloistered Emperor|1=Cloistered Emperor}}, and later to independent Kumano pilgrimages among the Kyoto nobility. Later, {{ill|Emperor Go-Shirakawa|en|Emperor Go-Shirakawa|WD=Q317984|lt=Emperor Go-Shirakawa|1=Emperor Go-Shirakawa}} also made 33 visits to Kumano. According to the diary of Fujiwara no Teika, who accompanied {{ill|Emperor Go-Toba|en|Emperor Go-Toba|WD=Q316658|lt=Emperor Go-Toba|1=Emperor Go-Toba}} on his Kumano pilgrimage in 1201 during the {{ill|Kamakura period|en|Kamakura period|WD=Q236205|lt=Kamakura period|1=Kamakura period}} (dd85-1333), the journey was made on foot in principle, with luggage carried on horseback, and the roads were maintained accordingly. During this period, the shrine was worshipped by the [[Minamoto clan|Minamoto]] and [[Taira clan]]s, and was visited by [[Ippen]] and {{ill|Mongaku|en|Mongaku|WD=Q11080166|lt=Mongaku|1=Mongaku}}, priests of the Heian and {{ill|Kamakura period|en|Kamakura period|WD=Q236205|lt=Kamakura period|1=Kamakura period}}s. {{ill|Hōjō Masako|en|Hōjō Masako|WD=Q463961|lt=Hojo Masako|1=Hōjō Masako}}, wife of [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]], also made two pilgrimages to Kumano on her way to Kyoto from Kamakura. Furthermore, after the {{ill|Jōkyū War|en|Jōkyū War|WD=Q1372308|lt=Jokyu Disturbance|1=Jōkyū War}} (1221), local samurai also began to make pilgrimages. == Kumano Sanzan == [[File:Kumano Kodo pilgrimage route Seiganto-ji World heritage 熊野古道 青岸渡寺02.JPG|alt=An image of Nachi Falls, part of the Kumano Nachi Taisha shrine complex, the waterfall is visible over a three-storied Buddhist pagoda.|thumb|Nachi Falls in the background of the Kumano Nachi Taisha shrine complex. The pagoda is [[Seiganto-ji]].]] {{Main|Kumano Sanzan}} The three great shrines which enshrine each of the Kumano Gongen are the guiding destinations of the pilgrimage. Each shrine has a particular focus for the benefits that the gods convey and the fortunes they bestow on the past, present, and future respectively. The shrines are highly visited today by visitors travelling via car, bus, and on foot. == Kumano faith == {{See also|Kumano shrine}} The Kumano Gongen are the deities that are revered by the Kumano faith. As a syncretic religion, the Kumano faith carries elements of [[Shinto]], [[Shugendō|Shugendo]], {{ill|Mountain worship|en|Mountain worship|WD=Q93697439|lt=Mountain worship|1=Mountain worship}}, and {{ill|Buddhism in Japan|en|Buddhism in Japan|WD=Q736311|lt=Buddhism|1=Buddhism in Japan}}, among others, and is sacred to each of these religions. They are themselves seen as aspects of their respective Shinto and Buddhist deities. They are embodied in natural wonders - [[Nachi Falls]], a giant boulder at Mount Gongenyama, and the sacred {{ill|Kumano River|en|Kumano River|WD=Q1972071|lt=Kumano River|1=Kumano River}}. The gods are said to have descended to Earth at a rock at the summit of Mount Gongenyama, which is adjacent to {{ill|Shingū, Wakayama|en|Shingū, Wakayama|WD=Q823526|lt=Shingu|1=Shingū, Wakayama}}. As the faith was proselytized throughout Japan, hundreds of local shrines were created to worship the Kumano gods. The faith was offered as one that is open to people from any background, especially to women who were banned from other sacred sites in Japan. Local shrines allowed the devout to worship the Kumano faith without having to take the extremely arduous journey to the Kumano Sanzan. The completion of the pilgrimage is said to automatically grant entrance into the {{ill|Bodhisattva|en|Bodhisattva|WD=Q178149|lt=Bodhisattva|1=Bodhisattva}} of compassion [[Kannon]]'s [[:en:Pure land|Pure land]] upon death.{{Citation |last=Suzuki |first=Masataka |title=The Localisation of Kumano Gongen Cult and Mountain Beliefs: From engi to kagura |date=2021-10-18 |url=https://edizionicafoscari.unive.it/it/edizioni/libri/978-88-6969-528-5/the-localisation-of-kumano-gongen-cult-and-mountai/ |work=Ca’ Foscari Japanese Studies |volume=14 |pages=Chapter_6402 |access-date=2023-05-12 |place=Venice |publisher=Fondazione Università Ca’ Foscari |doi=10.30687/978-88-6969-527-8/005 |isbn=978-88-6969-528-5|doi-access=free }} The holy land of the Kumano region increases in sacredness until reaching the epicentre at Hongu. The region itself can be seen as the land of the dead, or a pure land on Earth. For Shugendo practitioners, walking the routes through the sacred mountains form and reinforce sacred [[mandala]]s. {| class="wikitable" |+Table showing the syncretism of the Kumano deities !Grand Shrine !Buddhist deity !Shinto kami !Kumano deity !Natural object |- |[[Kumano Hongū Taisha|Hongu]] |[[:en:Amida Buddha|Amida]] |[[Susanoo-no-Mikoto|Susano-no-Mikoto]] |Ketsumiko-no-Okami |Trees, {{ill|Kumano River|en|Kumano River|WD=Q1972071|lt=Kumano-gawa River|1=Kumano River}}, Hongu sandbank, nature |- |[[Kumano Hayatama Taisha|Hayatama]] |[[:en:Yakushi|Yakushi]] |{{ill|Izanami|en|Izanami|WD=Q682306|lt=Izanagi-no-Mikoto|1=Izanami}}
Izanami-no-Mikoto |Kumano-Hayatama-no-Okami Kumano-Fusumi-no-Okami |Gotobiki-iwa rock (at [[Kamikura shine|Kamikura Shrine]], Shingu), Kumano-gawa River |- |[[Kumano Nachi Taisha|Nachi]] |{{ill|Thousand-armed Kannon|fr|Thousand-armed Kannon|ja|千手観音|lt=Thousand-Armed Kannon}} |{{ill|Izanami|en|Izanami|WD=Q682306|lt=Izanami|1=Izanami}} |Kumano-Fusumi-no-Okami |[[Nachi Falls]] |} === Buddhist elements === [[File:Yamabushi-Omini-Okugakemichi-Yoshino.jpg|alt=Monks with cropped hair and walking staves hiking up a steep mountain trail in white robes.|thumb|Yamabushi on the Omine route.]]The Kumano Gongen are similar to many other gods in Japan, in that they are understood by Buddhists, under the principle of [[honji suijaku]], to be incarnations of buddhas and bodhisattvas. In fact, the word gongen means a buddha manifesting as a [[kami]]. There are many Buddhist elements throughout the Kumano Kodo, including hundreds of small Jizo and Kannon statues on the routes, the Kohechi route to the Buddhist centre of Koyasan, the belief in the Kumano region as a pure land, and the co-existence of {{ill|Buddhist temples in Japan|en|Buddhist temples in Japan|WD=Q3141900|lt=Buddhist temples|1=Buddhist temples in Japan}} within the grand shrine precincts (such as [[Seiganto-ji]]). There are many important Buddhist sites along the routes, including mounds with [[Stupa|stupas]] on top where Buddhist scriptures were buried in order to preserve them and obtain {{ill|Merit (Buddhism)|en|Merit (Buddhism)|WD=Q1406348|lt=merit|1=Merit (Buddhism)}} for the preserver.{{Cite book |title=Kumano Kodo Official Guide Book}} === Shugendo elements === [[Shugendō|Shugendo]] monks ([[Yamabushi]]) have served as guides on the trail since ancient times and form an integral part of the religion of the area. [[Mount Tamaki]] and {{ill|Mount Ōmine|en|Mount Ōmine|WD=Q3695989|lt=Mount Ōmine|1=Mount Ōmine}} are just two of the sacred mountains with significant Shugendo presence in the region. === Shinto elements === [[File:GOOUHONGUU.JPG|alt=A talisman in the form of ricepaper that has been stamped with kanji symbols except the symbols are made of crows.|thumb|[[:ja:熊野牛王符|Gyuoh Hoin]] talisman from Kumano Hongu Taisha.]] {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|WD=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrines|1=Shinto shrine}} (jinja) are extremely common throughout the region and on the trails. Some of the most common shrines in the region hold the gods [[Susanoo-no-Mikoto|Susano]], [[Amaterasu|Ametarasu]] and {{ill|Inari shrine|en|Inari shrine|WD=Q514480|lt=Inari|1=Inari shrine}}. There are also many shrines that contain local kami, and kami that inhabit natural features. Some of these shrines hold the spirits of Imperial officials and warriors, or have stories pertaining to imperial pilgrimages. The pilgrimage became popular among boatbuilders and fishermen as it is said to be where Susano created the first boat after witnessing a drowning spider climb onto a leaf. The Kumano Gongen are also understood as manifestations of Shinto deities, in the same way that the Buddhist deities are. This is an example of [[shinbutsu-shūgō]], or Buddhist-Shinto syncretism. There are also many {{ill|Yōkai|en|Yōkai|WD=Q503186|lt=yokai|1=Yōkai}} said to inhabit the region. Among these are the daru spirits, serpentine witch beings who can turn invisible and penetrate a pilgrim's body to apply physical torments. [[File:Yatagarasu, Kumano Nachi Taisha.jpg|alt=A hanging fabric at Kumano Nachi Taisha, depicting two three-legged crows holding a plant.|thumb|A depiction of Yatagarasu at Kumano Nachi Taisha.]] === Yatagarasu === {{Main articles|Yatagarasu}} Yagarasu, the three-legged crow, is a ubiquitous symbol of the [[Kumano Region|Kumano region]]. They have a dedicated shrine at the Kumano Nachii Taisha complex. This crow god is said to have been sent from heaven as a guide for legendary {{ill|Emperor Jimmu|en|Emperor Jimmu|WD=Q200188|lt=Emperor Jimmu|1=Emperor Jimmu}} on his last climactic battle to become the first Japanese Emperor; together they travelled from Shingu in the Kumano region to what would become {{ill|Yamato Province|en|Yamato Province|WD=Q907495|lt=Yamato|1=Yamato Province}}.{{Cite web |title=The Yatagarasu: The Three-legged Crow That Guided Emperor Jimmu on his Journey |url=https://www.kokugakuin.ac.jp/en/article/145336 |access-date=2023-05-12 |website=國學院大學 |language=en}} Crows are depicted on the sacred [[:ja:熊野牛王符|Gyuoh Hoin]] (熊野牛王符) amulets and {{ill|Omamori|en|Omamori|WD=Q1756788|lt=Omamori|1=Omamori}} available at the shrines.{{Cite web |last=Greve |first=Gabi |date=20dd-09-14 |title=Omamori - Japanese Amulets: Kumano and Nachi amulets |url=https://omamorifromjapan.blogspot.com/20dd/09/kumano-and-nachi-amulets.html |access-date=2023-05-12 |website=Omamori - Japanese Amulets}} === Kōshin === {{Main articles|Kōshin}} While not as popular today, the ancient Kōshin religion persists along the Kumano Kodo in the form of monuments and shrines. One of the central features of this religion is the belief that three parasites live in the human body and will ascend to heaven once a month to report the person's sins. As this occurred at night, it became custom to stay awake and revel all night on this day each month. == Oji shrines == [[File:Takijiri-oji shrine 2.jpg|alt=An image of Takijiri-oji shrine, the formal entryway into the holy land of Kumano. It is a wooden shrine building with stone lanterns in the front set against forested mountains.|thumb|Takijiri-oji shrine, the formal entryway into the holy land of Kumano.]] The 99 'princes' are shrines which were established mainly from the 12th to 13th centuries. These are found from Watanobe-tsu (Kubotsu, Kuhonetsu) at the mouth of the {{ill|Yodo River|en|Yodo River|WD=Q1140505|lt=Yodo River|1=Yodo River}}, which was the base of the Kumano Kodō (especially Kii-ji and Nakabe-ji) in Osaka, to the Kumano Sanzan (three mountains). Pilgrims walked to the Kumano Sanzan, resting at the 99 Oji shrines. Few of them still exist today in their original condition. == Routes == There are many routes that make up the broader Kumano Kodō pilgrimage. Not all of these routes are intended to be traversed in one trip, as they originate from different locations, and some lesser known routes are not in use. Additionally, not all of the routes have World Heritage status either. The name Kumano Kodō today primarily refers to the following six main roads: * Kiiji (Watanobe-tsu - Tanabe) * Kohechi (Koyasan - Kumano Sanzan, approx. 70 km) * Nakahechi (Tanabe - Kumano Sanzan) * Ohechi (Tanabe - Kushimoto - Kumano Sanzan, approx. 120 km) * Iseji (Ise Jingu - Kumano Sanzan, approx. 160 km) * Omine Okugakemichi (Yoshino - Kumano Sanzan). === Kiiji === The ''Kiiji'' route runs along the west coast of the peninsula from {{ill|Kyoto|en|Kyoto|WD=Q34600|lt=Kyoto|1=Kyoto}} to {{ill|Tanabe, Wakayama|en|Tanabe, Wakayama|WD=Q304266|lt=Tanabe|1=Tanabe, Wakayama}}, where it forks into two more routes: Nakahechi; and Ohechi. The Kiiji route was frequented by the emperors as they travelled many times throughout their lives from the imperial capital of Kyoto. Today, the majority of the Kiiji route is paved roads and rural and urban areas that show little resemblance to the past. It is not part of the World Heritage listing. === Ohechi === The ''Ohechi'' route continues south along the coast from Tanabe to Shingu. While there is tourist information available for this route, it is not frequently travelled today and is primarily freeways which can make it dangerous for a walker to traverse. The Ohechi route is more modern than the other routes and was established as an easier route to bypass the mountains. === Nakahechi === [[File:Kumano Kodo Kumano Hongu Taisha World heritage 熊野本宮大社18.JPG|alt=An image of the entrance of Kumano Hongu Taisha, a torii gate stands prominently in front of tall green trees. To the side are Japanese paper lanterns, and a prominent banner stands in front of a three-legged-crow.|thumb|The entrance to Kumano Hongu Taisha and terminus of the first leg of the Nakahechi.]] The Nakahechi route leads into the rugged interior mountains toward Kumano Hongū Taisha. The main route covers the distance from Tanabe to {{ill|Hongū, Wakayama|en|Hongū, Wakayama|WD=Q2251838|lt=Hongū|1=Hongū, Wakayama}} and then the Nakahechi continues on to Nachi and Shingu. From Hongū, most pilgrims would take a boat down the Kumano River to The ''Nakahechi'' route was the most popular for pilgrimages from Kyoto, the ancient capital of Japan. The earliest records of this route dates from the early 10th century. The trail has a long history of use by people with diverse belief backgrounds, leading to mixed religious symbolism overlaid and incorporated into the setting and stages of the pilgrimage. The UNESCO World Heritage registered section begins at Takijiri-oji, which is considered to be the point of entry to the sacred area of Kumano. From here it is about 40 km of mountainous trail before one reaches Kumano Hongū Taisha. Most pilgrimages break the journey into a two-day walk. The town of Chikatsuyu is about halfway. Most pilgrims stay the night here at a [[Ryokan (inn)#Minshuku|minshuku]]. ==== Dainichi-goe and Akagi-goe ==== [[File:Kumano Kodo World heritage Yunomine Onsen Tsuboyu 湯の峰温泉 つぼ湯06.JPG|alt=An image of a hot spring bath carved out of rock in a wooden building.|thumb|215x215px|Tsuboyu, ancient onsen at Yunomine.]] The Kumano Kodō ''Dainichi-goe'' route links the [[Kumano Hongū Taisha]] with {{ill|Yunomine Onsen|en|Yunomine Onsen|WD=Q11563414|lt=Yunomine|1=Yunomine Onsen}}. It is 2 km long and a steep climb. It descends over a small pass. Pilgrims often did purification rites at the Yunomine {{ill|Onsen|en|Onsen|WD=Q655311|lt=Onsen|1=Onsen}} (Yunomine hot spring). Tsuboyu is a small cabin on the creek that runs through this isolated village, featuring a small rocky bath that is the only World Heritage hot spring open to visitors. The bath was used for purification rites and its legendary healing effects. The ''Akagi-goe'' is a relatively recent route that was established within the last few hundred years to reach Yunomine onsen more quickly from the west before continuing onto {{ill|Hongū, Wakayama|en|Hongū, Wakayama|WD=Q2251838|lt=Hongū|1=Hongū, Wakayama}}. It covers 6.5 km from Mikoshi-toge pass to Yunomine onsen and is a relatively leisurely walk along steep mountain ridges. There are no oji on the route. Modern pilgims may combine these walks into a circular path that loops back around to Hongū over a day. ==== Kumano-gawa ==== The Kumano-gawa was the primary route continuing on from the 'main route' of the Nakahechi. From the Kumano Hongū Taisha, most pilgrims went by boat on the Kumano River to [[Kumano Hayatama Taisha]] in the coastal town of {{ill|Shingū, Wakayama|en|Shingū, Wakayama|WD=Q823526|lt=Shingū|1=Shingū, Wakayama}}. This 40 km section of the Kumano Kodō is the only river pilgrimage route that is registered as a World Heritage site. Today, the route is seasonally serviced by a traditional boat tour from March to November. Pilgrims would then double back to Nachi to visit the Kumano Nachi Taisha. ==== Kogumotori-goe and Ogumotori-goe ==== [[File:Kumano Kodo World heritage Ohgumotorigoe 熊野古道 大雲取越dd4.JPG|alt=An image of a steep path with roughhewn cobblestones through a pine forest plantation, the road is old and very worn.|thumb|Steep cobblestones on the Ogumotori-goe road.]] These overland routes links the Kumano Hongū Taisha with the [[Kumano Nachi Taisha]]. Most pilgrims take two days to complete this walk, staying overnight in the small town of Koguchi. The section between Hongū and Koguchi is called the Kogumotori-goe. The section between Koguchi and Kumano Nachi Taisha is called the Ogumotori-goe and features the hardest part of the whole pilgrimage, the Dogiri-zaka or 'backbreaking slope' which climbs one kilometre in elevation. ==== Nachi to Shingu ==== [[File:Fudarakusanji02s1024.jpg|alt=A reproduction of a sealed wooden boat.|thumb|A reproduction of a boat used by the Fudarakusanji monks setting off for the southern pure land.]] From Nachi, a pilgrim can continue onwards to finish their pilgrimage in Shingu. This route travels from Nachi through rural suburbs until reaching the seaside town of {{ill|Nachikatsuura|en|Nachikatsuura|WD=Q1346730|lt=Nachikatsuura|1=Nachikatsuura}}, where [[Fudarakusan-ji]] temple is located. This temple was a base for Kumano monks who would be sealed in enclosed boats with a small amount of supplies and sent off into the {{ill|Philippine Sea|en|Philippine Sea|WD=Q159183|lt=Philippine Sea|1=Philippine Sea}} to find the southern [[:en:Pure land|Pure land]]. Here, pilgrims would perform salt-water purification. The route then continues roughly perpendicular to the coast and [[:en:Kinokuni Line|Kinokuni JR train-line]] and follows {{ill|Japan National Route 42|en|Japan National Route 42|WD=Q2003243|lt=the freeway|1=Japan National Route 42}} and local streets. While today most people take a bus from Nachi, there are further World Heritage passes including the ruins of the Monkey Tea House and the Koyazaka Slope which can only be reached on foot while travelling from Nachi through [[Ugui, Wakayama|Ugui]] and onwards to Shingu. === Kohechi === {{See also|Mount Kōya}} [[File:Koyasan (Mount Koya) monks.jpg|alt=An image of monks in orange robes walking on a stone path with Buddhist monuments in the background.|thumb|Buddhist monks at Mount Koya, the start of the Kohechi route.]] The "Kohechi" route links {{ill|Mount Kōya|en|Mount Kōya|WD=Q535065|lt=Koyasan|1=Mount Kōya}} to the [[Kumano shrine#Kumano Sanzan|Kumano Sanzan]]. It runs north to south and is 70 km long. It is the shortest route connecting Koyasan to Kumano. It is a tough walk, that traverses three passes of over 1,000 meters elevation gain. === Iseji === {{Main|Iseji (Kumano Kodō)}} {{See also|Ise Grand Shrine}} [[File:Ise grand shrine Naiku , 伊勢神宮 内宮 - panoramio (dd).jpg|alt=An image of Ise Grand Shrine Naikū, one of the large wooden shrines that make up the most sacred Shinto site in Japan. The site enshrines Amaterasu and there are many imperial symbols visible.|thumb|Ise Grand Shrine Naikū]] The "Iseji" route links [[Ise Grand Shrine]] with the Kumano Sanzan. In the 17th century this route became part of the {{ill|Saigoku Kannon Pilgrimage|en|Saigoku Kannon Pilgrimage|WD=Q750721|lt=Saikogu pilgrimage|1=Saigoku Kannon Pilgrimage}}. The first temple is [[Seiganto-ji]], which is closely related to the [[Kumano Nachi Taisha]]. Some pilgrims (ohenro) also combine the Iseji route with the {{ill|Shikoku Pilgrimage|en|Shikoku Pilgrimage|WD=Q1972399|lt=Shikoku pilgrimage|1=Shikoku Pilgrimage}}, starting from Ise Grand Shrine and following the Iseji to the Nakahechi and onwards to Shikoku. The "Magose Toge" forms the boundary between {{ill|Miyama, Kyoto|en|Miyama, Kyoto|WD=Q6884300|lt=Miyama, Kyoto|1=Miyama, Kyoto}} and [[:en:Owase, Mie|Owase, Mie]]. A moss-covered stone path stretches about 2 km into the beautiful cypress forest covered with ferns. This route leads to Tengura-san with a huge stone at the tip. A small tunnel below the stone can be entered. From the stone is a scenic view of {{ill|Owase|en|Owase|WD=Q847554|lt=Owase City|1=Owase}}. Magose-koen Park on the way down the pass is renowned for its [[:en:Cherry blossoms|Cherry blossoms]].Revival of the Ancient Pilgrimage Road{{clarify|date=October 2019}} Today, much of the Iseji walk is on paved roads through urban and rural coastal areas. === Ōmine Okugakemichi === {{Main|Ōmine Okugakemichi}} {{See also|Mount Ōmine}} [[File:Mount Misen and Omine Mountains.jpg|alt=An image of the forest covered hills of Mount Omine and Mount Misen, the rolling mountains are popularly likened to the waves of the sea stretching to the horizon.|thumb|Mount Ōmine next to Mount Misen, an example of the 'ocean of mountains' in the region.]] The route connecting {{ill|Mount Ōmine|en|Mount Ōmine|WD=Q3695989|lt=Mount Ōmine|1=Mount Ōmine}} to the Kumano Sanzan is an extremely steep and difficult one traversed by [[yamabushi]] ([[Shugendō|Shugendo]] monks) of Shogo-in temple in Kyoto as part of their religious practice. In winter the route is so dangerous that even the yamabushi do not generally travel it. On this route ascetic practices such as immersion in frozen waterfalls are conducted by the monks. Women travelling the route must bypass Mount Ōmine itself as it is forbidden for women to enter. == Rediscovered routes == There were many routes in the Kii Peninsula that have become hidden or lost over time, but while these are not part of the World Heritage designation, they may also be considered part of the Kumano Kodō. === Okuhechi === Okuhechi (奥辺路) is a forgotten seventh Kumano Kodō (pilgrimage route) to Kumano Hongu Taisha Shrine currently being researched and developed. The route from {{ill|Mount Kōya|en|Mount Kōya|WD=Q535065|lt=Koyasan|1=Mount Kōya}}, passes through Gomadanzan and {{ill|Ryujin Onsen|en|Ryujin Onsen|WD=Q11679329|lt=Ryujin Onsen|1=Ryujin Onsen}}, branching off at the foot of Kasatayama, crossing the {{ill|Hatenashi Sanmyaku Prefectural Natural Park|en|Hatenashi Sanmyaku Prefectural Natural Park|WD=Q105360015|lt=Hatenashi|1=Hatenashi Sanmyaku Prefectural Natural Park}} range along the Niu River, and joining the Kohechi at Totsukawa Onsen. The route then continues south to join the Nakahechi. Although it runs parallel to the west side of the Kohechi, it passes through Koya-cho, Katsuragi-cho, Aritagawa-cho, and Tanabe City in Wakayama Prefecture according to the current administrative divisions (the latter half of the route that crosses the Hatenashi Mountains enters Nara Prefecture). Its existence has been remembered and passed down by local elders, and local volunteers have been working to identify and maintain the buried old road, referring to the description in the town magazine of the former Shimizu Town.{{Cite web |title=奥辺路プロジェクトとは？ {{!}} 龍神村 {{!}} DragonsVillage {{!}} 龍のむら {{!}} 龍の里づくり {{!}} 日本 |url=https://www.dragongodvillagejapan.com/okuhejiproject |access-date=2023-04-27 |website=Dragonsvillage |language=ja}} === Ogurimichi === There is a forgotten eighth road, Ogurimichi, which runs from southern Osaka to Kumano Hongu via Tanabe City. It is a popular name derived from the legend of the revival of [[Ogurihangan]]. The route was used from the Edo period to the beginning of the {{ill|Shōwa era|en|Shōwa era|WD=Q327567|lt=Showa period|1=Shōwa era}} by disabled people and people suffering from {{ill|leprosy|en|leprosy|WD=Q36956|lt=leprosy|1=Leprosy}}. These people would travel to Kumano Hongu Shrine and the Yunomine Onsen baths in the hope of being cured of their illnesses. The section of the Oguri that is parallel to the Nakahechi is isolated from the general pilgrims as it was considered {{ill|Purity in Buddhism|en|Purity in Buddhism|WD=Q1583270|lt=impure|1=Purity in Buddhism}}. This section is considered to be in particularly good condition. The Oguri Road reveals the more negative aspects of the Kumano Kodō, a pilgrimage on which many would die while travelling it, but it also shows the depth and diversity of the Kumano faith which has been open to the prayers of many different people.{{Cite book |author= |title=Biocity 90 号（特集：世界遺産条約50周年・日本批准30周年 世界遺産の歴史と未来像） |publisher=ブックエンド |year=2022 |isbn=978-4907083755 |page=128}} == Geography == One of the features of the Kumano Kodō is that the original stone pavement remains in many areas, such as the Daimonzaka slope. The reason for the use of cobblestones is that the Kii Peninsula is one of the areas in Japan with the highest rainfall. There are many historic sites such as village ruins, teahouse and inn ruins, gravesites, markers of Imperial visits, Ichirizuka (waypoint mounds maintained by the Kishu Clan during the Edo Period), shrines, and Buddhist stupas where scrolls were buried. Some of the Kumano Kodō routes overlap with national roads and urban routes and have been paved and shared with cars. For example, the route formerly known as the Totsukawa Kaido has been absorbed into Route 168 and most of the Ohechi and Iseji routes overlap with National Route 42. The reason why the Kiiji route is not World Heritage registered is because it was repaired and widened as a prefectural road and a mountain trail. This is related to the geography of the Kii Peninsula. The central part of the Kii Peninsula is covered with endless mountains and valleys, although there are no prominent high mountains. For this reason, it has been difficult since ancient times to develop transportation, and the places suitable for traffic have been limited. This is still the case today, and as a result, the main modern transportation routes parallel or overlap with the paths pioneered by the ancients. Examples of parallel routes include the Nakahechi and National Route 3dd, the Kii Peninsula portion of the JR Kisei Main Line and National Route 42, and the Ohechi and Iseji roads. There are also exceptions such as Kobeji and Omine Okugakemichi. == World Heritage Site registration == [[File:Kumano Kodo Dainichigoe World heritage04.JPG|alt=An image of people walking on a gravel forested path, the central focus is a large rock monument with a brass plate commemorating the establishment of the UNESCO World Heritage site.|thumb|243x243px|UNESCO World Heritage monument on the Dainichigoe road.]] In 2004, Kumano Kodō was registered as a World Heritage Site by UNESCO as part of "Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range" ("Monuments and Cultural Landscapes" under "Cultural Heritage"). This was the first time in Japan that a road was registered as a World Heritage site, and the second case of a World Heritage site as a whole, following the "Pilgrimage Route of Santiago de Compostela" in Spain. However, the Kii Road is not included in the list of World Heritage sites. Kiiji was the most frequently used road until the present day, and as a result of gradual structural improvements to the road over the course of history, it inevitably lost its appearance as a pilgrimage route in the past, making it difficult to be accepted as a World Heritage site. The World Heritage list is not the entirety of the Kumano Kodō. This is due to the following reasons: the exact route of the Kumano pilgrimage itself has waxed and waned, and some sections of the route are still unknown; some of the routes are derived from historical changes, and not all of them are included; some sections have to be detoured when rivers rise; and some coastal "roads" are not safe to travel along. There is a local movement to rediscover other "forgotten" routes of the Kumano Kodō. === Sister pilgrimage with the Camino de Santiago === Galicia, Spain, the final destination of the "{{ill|Camino de Santiago|en|Camino de Santiago|WD=Q41150|lt=Pilgrimage Route to Santiago de Compostela|1=Camino de Santiago}}," a World Heritage Site, and Wakayama Prefecture, the final destination of the Kumano Kodō, concluded a sister road affiliation on October 9, 1998, in order to establish a lasting friendly relationship as the final destination of both ancient pilgrimage routes[7]. 7]. Since then, "Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range," including the Kumano Kodō, have also been registered as UNESCO World Heritage sites, thus continuing the exchange between the World Heritage sites of the roads [Note 3]. Pilgrims that have completed both the Spanish and Japanese pilgrimages can receive a certificate of 'Dual-pilgrimage'. ==Gallery== Daimonzaka28-640.jpg|Daimonzaka. Kumano Kodō (Japan 2007 250).jpg|Part of the Kumano Kodō near the {{ill|Yunomine Onsen|en|Yunomine Onsen|WD=Q11563414|lt=Yunomine Onsen|1=Yunomine Onsen}}. Kumano Kodō (Japan 2007 dd8).jpg|A traveler on the Kumano Kodō. Kumano Kodo 8.jpg|The Kumano Kodō near Hosshinmon-oji. Kumano Kodo 3.jpg|A small shrine near Takahara village. Kumano Kodo 6.jpg|The Kumano Kodō near Tsugizakura-oji. Kumano Kodo 5.jpg|A religious monument near Hisohara-oji. Kumano Kodo 9.jpg|An old milestone for 1 ri — around 4 km, on the Kumano Kodō. Kumano Kodo 2.jpg|The route near the [[Kumano Hongū Taisha]]. Kumano Kodo 7.jpg|A {{ill|Kṣitigarbha|en|Kṣitigarbha|WD=Q604687|lt=Kṣitigarbha|1=Kṣitigarbha}} figure inside the small shrine at Inohana-oji. ==See also== *{{ill|Japan 100 Kannon Pilgrimage|en|Japan 100 Kannon Pilgrimage|WD=Q10312302|lt=Japan 100 Kannon Pilgrimage|1=Japan 100 Kannon Pilgrimage}} *{{ill|Shikoku Pilgrimage|en|Shikoku Pilgrimage|WD=Q1972399|lt=Shikoku Pilgrimage|1=Shikoku Pilgrimage}} *{{ill|Tourism in Japan|en|Tourism in Japan|WD=Q1060220|lt=Tourism in Japan|1=Tourism in Japan}} *{{ill|The 100 Views of Nature in Kansai|en|The 100 Views of Nature in Kansai|WD=Q11656381|lt=The 100 Views of Nature in Kansai|1=The 100 Views of Nature in Kansai}} *[[Shugendō]] *[[Kumano shrine]] ==Notes== {{reflist|group=Note}} == References == {{reflist|1}} ==Bibliography== * {{citation |title=Kumano Kodo Travel Guide |last=Beumer |first=Hans |date=2016 }}. == External links == *[https://www.hikemasterjapan.com/kumanokodo A guide to hiking the famous Nakahechi route] *[http://www.tb-kumano.jp/en/ Tanabe City Kumano Tourism Bureau] *[http://www.kumadoco.net/kodo_eng/about/index.html#no2 Iseji information] *[https://www.shinguu.jp/en Shingu City Tourist Association] *[https://visitnara.jp/lists-and-stories/story/hiking-nara's-pilgrimage-routes/ Kumano Kodō, from The Official Nara Travel Guide] *[http://www.kumanokodocenter.com/10dd17.html Kumano Kodō Center] in Owase {{Walking routes}} {{coord missing|Wakayama Prefecture}} {{Kumano Faith}} [[en:Kumano Kodō]] [[es:Kumano Kodo]] [[fr:Kumano kodō]] [[it:Kumano Kodō]] [[ja:熊野古道]] [[pt:Kumano Kodō]] [[ru:Кумано-кодо]] [[zh:熊野古道]] {{wikidata link|Q17050475}} [[Category:History of Wakayama Prefecture]] [[Category:Japanese pilgrimages]] [[Category:Roads in Wakayama Prefecture]] [[Category:Tourist attractions in Wakayama Prefecture]] [[Category:Wikidata has short description]] [[Category:World Heritage Sites in Japan]]
